**What is this project about?**  
**It is a game simulation where an avatar has to learn the unknown roles of the object it sees in its environment. It has to figure out these roles and find a way to navigate to the goal object to get the reward. This is a form of theory based reinforcement learning done via Bayesian learning and generational knowledge transfer across agents. This experiment shows how generational knowledge transfer speeds up the learning process and how using a probability model sampling framework can result in the Hot-Stove effect.**

**![][image1]**  
**My claim was:**  
**Literal learner:**  
**Oracle\>No-advice\>Selective\>Guess**  
This claim is mostly true but I had not taken into account how selective performs better than no-advice. This might be due to the fact that the goal touches occur more in this experiment than false warnings which leads to useful knowledge transfer to the next agent.  
**Calibrates learner:**  
**Oracle\>Best-Guess\>Selective\>No-Advice**  
**This claim holds as predicted**

**Link to Summary Table**  
[https\://github.com/thegamerpopz/RLProject/blob/eec1a35484f46ad977aba09ffdc36030d6e6f135/gridworld/results/summary.csv](https://github.com/thegamerpopz/RLProject/blob/eec1a35484f46ad977aba09ffdc36030d6e6f135/gridworld/results/summary.csv)  
The warning touched is exceptionally high for budget 1 calibrated learner as due to tie breaker rule the best\_guess returns lethal and the explorer takes a random move as it is mostly below the threshold danger we have set. However in comparison for budget 1 literal learner it will be assigned lethal and avoided which is why we see such warning\_never dominating.  
In most cases the warning blocks are avoided thus demonstrating the hot stove effect.  
The endorsement\_touched in all columns is more as the explorer does not avoid the endorsements and does not discriminate them against a blank block per se. 

I would conclude that false warnings are more harmful for the learning algorithm.

Calibrated learner- As the first win mean  lies between 1.12\[calibrated and oracle\] and 3.45\[no\_advice\] in all cases we can say for sure there is a benefit from the advice given by the previous generation and this benefit increases as we increase the number of episodes and only allow selective advice to pass through.

Literal learner-This shows a similar trend however there is one exception. In literal best\_guess the advice is detrimental as due to the noise in the data and the amplification of it by literal learner wrong information is continuously passed through several times which in case of false warnings leads to the hot stove effect. This can be seen by the average win rate for it being 7.87 compared to no advice which is 0.85.
